title: The Question–Behaviour Effect
description: Asking a question instead of making a statement makes people far more likely to act.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: A statement invites agreement or disagreement. A question invites the mind to search for reasons to say yes. Simply turning "you should vote" into "will you vote?" sharply raises the number who do.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: A question prompts an internal search for a reason to comply, and it nudges the person to picture themselves doing the thing — which makes the action feel more like their own idea.

sections.title: Real-Life Examples
content: "Will you vote on Tuesday?" outperformed "Please vote on Tuesday."
"Are you going to help with this?" gathers more hands than "We need help."

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: Requests phrased as questions about the person's own future behaviour.
A gentle "will you…" in place of a direct instruction.

sections.title: Ethical Uses
sections.content: Turning a genuine request into a question respects the other person's autonomy while making the ask clearer.

sections.title: Manipulative Uses
sections.content: Engineering a "yes" through leading questions that bypass the person's real preferences.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: A question that is really a command in disguise.

sections.title: Defense Strategies
content: Notice when a question is steering you toward a commitment.
It is fine to answer "no" to a question — you have not agreed to anything yet.

sections.title: Mistakes People Make
content: Assuming only assertive statements persuade. Questions often work better.
Missing that you have effectively promised something by answering a question.

sections.title: Key Lessons
content: A question makes people rehearse the action.
Watch what you commit to when you answer.
